newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UBS says Swiss Holocaust fund makes business sense.
newsitem.headline: UBS says Swiss Holocaust fund makes business sense.

text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) on Thursday cited worries that a U.S. backlash could hurt its business as part of the reason it joined Switzerland's other biggest banks to create a Holocaust memorial fund.

UBS chairman Robert Studer told shareholders there were business reasons as well as humanitarian motives in donating 100 million Swiss francs ($68 million) together with rivals Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC).

He also said the fund should pay any legal damages that could arise from three huge class-action suits that Holocaust victims have filed in U.S. courts seeking billions from Swiss banks for allegedly hoarding unclaimed Jewish wealth.

The three banks in February were the first to donate money for a humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors that the Swiss government then formally created using the cash and another 165 million francs from private companies and the central bank.
"As shareholders of the bank you may be asking yourselves how we can justify this kind of donation," Studer said at the annual shareholder meeting.

The donation was a gesture of good will, he said, "but we are not about to conceal the fact that this gesture is also strongly motivated by our business activities in the U.S., which are important for the overall performance of UBS," Studer said.
"Our position there (the U.S.) and our reputation, on which banking relationships are largely based, are at stake and are being increasingly called into question," he said.
"While our contribution to the humanitarian fund is certainly justifiable on ethical and moral grounds, there is also a business rationale to it," Studer added.
Studer made clear the fund should handle any claims Swiss banks might be forced to pay as a result of the class-action suits, adding UBS had made no provisions for any such payments.
"Any potential claims will have to be settled from this (fund)," Studer said in the first public comment from a senior Swiss banker suggesting the fund could be used for this end.

The memorial fund and broader government plan to create a seven billion Swiss franc foundation to help the world's poor and persecuted came about in the past two months under mounting pressure led by U.S.-based Jewish groups and U.S. politicians.

At the crux of the controversy are Jewish claims that Swiss banks withheld accounts left by Holocaust victims and that Switzerland generally profited from its status as a neutral financial centre during World War Two.

New York city and state considered barring public business with Swiss banks and other state and local authorities have voiced similar threats, although the World Jewish Congress (WJC) dropped boycott plans after the Holocaust fund was created.
UBS spokeswoman Gerturd Erismann said it made sense to settle any future damages from the fund because the class-action suits were aimed against Swiss banks in general.

Erismann said UBS was in negotiations with the plaintiffs in the U.S., but added these talks had so far been limited to points of legal procedure about how the cases should be tried and whether the banks would have to disclose all their records.
Erismann said there had been no talks as yet with the U.S. plaitiffs about the substance of the suits or the possibility of out-of-court settlements. ($ = 1.47 Swiss Francs)
